Re: Q4 2019 Follow-Up Report - ApexHip MDR Trending per 2019-05-08 Correspondence

Dear Sir or Madam:

In accordance with the schedule set forth in our May 8, 2019 correspondence concerning medical device reporting and complaint trending for the ApexHip Metal-on-Metal Total Hip System, cleared under K162447, Veridian Orthopedics is submitting this follow-up report.

For the reporting period that concluded on September 30, 2019, Veridian’s post-market complaint-data review shows an ApexHip complaint rate of 0.34%, calculated from complaints received in relation to distributed units. Reports of pain, elevated metal-ion findings, and revision procedures remain among the complaints. The Quality organization assesses every complaint separately under Veridian’s complaint-handling procedures and the applicable requirements of 21 CFR Part 820.

Veridian has maintained its periodic trend analysis, reviewing complaint narratives, available clinical information, returned-product information when available, and Medical Device Report determinations pursuant to 21 CFR Part 803. When the information available reasonably indicates that a reportable event has taken place, MDRs are submitted. If further relevant information is obtained, follow-up information is submitted as appropriate.

At the same time, Veridian’s engineering organization continues to evaluate wear characteristics across various implantation conditions, including higher acetabular cup inclination angles. The purpose of this effort is to improve our understanding of how surgical positioning and implant-use conditions relate to post-market observations. This evaluation is ongoing and is being examined through our established design and quality processes.

For now, Veridian will continue enhanced surveillance of ApexHip complaints and trend data. In accordance with applicable regulations, we will notify FDA of significant changes in complaint patterns, reportability assessments, or other information requiring notification. Unless material information calls for earlier communication, we will also issue another status update in the first quarter of 2020.

Should FDA need any additional information, please contact me.

Respectfully,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
4400 Silver Lake Blvd
Warsaw, Indiana 46580

June 22, 2022

Northgate Health System
Attn: Risk Management / Materials Management
Re: URGENT — Voluntary Recall Notification
ApexHip Acetabular Cup, Lots V-2200 through V-2299
FDA Recall Number: Z-1418-2022

Dear Risk Management Colleague:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is issuing this letter as formal notice of the voluntary recall of ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299. These lots were produced at our Cork, Ireland facility between November 2021 and February 2022. The FDA has designated this action as a Class II recall under recall number Z-1418-2022.

The recall began when incoming inspections at two hospital sites found that the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating flaked during removal from the sterile package, before implantation. Our investigation concluded that, after a chamber maintenance event, drift in a plasma-spray process parameter caused inconsistent adhesion of the coating in the affected lots. To date, 1,140 units from these lots have been distributed, and approximately 412 have been implanted.

Northgate Health System is requested to take these actions immediately:

1. Locate and quarantine every remaining unimplanted unit from lots V-2200 through V-2299 in your inventory.
2. Ensure that quarantined units are not used in surgical procedures.
3. Record the results of your inventory review on the enclosed Effectiveness Check Response Form and return it to our Regulatory Affairs department within 10 business days of the date of this letter.
4. Arrange the return and replacement of quarantined stock at no cost by contacting your Veridian sales representative or Customer Quality at 1-800-555-0142.

Should any patients with implanted units have experienced adverse events that may be associated with coating integrity, report them through your standard adverse event process and also inform our Complaint Handling department.

We apologize for any disruption this may create and value your prompt cooperation. Please contact me directly if you have questions.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
VP, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
dokonkwo@veridianortho.com

Enclosure: Effectiveness Check Response Form

[full text of the June 25, 2021 Form 483 transmittal letter, as previously circulated, quoted in full below]

RE: FDA Form 483 — Inspectional Observations
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc., Warsaw, Indiana Facility
Inspection Dates: June 14–18, 2021
FEI Number: 3003847215

Dear Ms. Okonkwo:

The observations identified during the inspection of your firm's facility by the undersigned Investigator on the dates stated above are transmitted in this letter pursuant to Section 704 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. They are provided at the inspection’s conclusion and are not a final Agency determination concerning your compliance. The inspectional observations are as follows:

Observation 1: For complaint investigations examined from calendar years 2019–2021, the records did not consistently show the date on which complaint information was received, making it insufficiently documented whether reportability decisions under 21 CFR 803.50 occurred within the required timeframes. In particular, seven of the twenty-two complaint files reviewed (TrackWise records) did not establish when your firm first became aware of information reasonably indicating a reportable event, preventing verification that the 30-day MDR submission requirement was met.

Observation 2: CAPA record CAPA-2019-041, opened in response to a 2019 coating adhesion issue, lacked documented effectiveness-check information or subsequent verification demonstrating that the corrective action implemented effectively prevented recurrence, as required under 21 CFR 820.100(a)(4).

Observation 3: The document-control procedures governing labeling revisions did not consistently show approval signatures and effective dates before the revisions were released for use, as required under 21 CFR 820.40. This issue was identified in one of the five labeling change records reviewed.

The observations listed on this Form 483 were made by the FDA representative(s) during the inspection of your facility. They are inspectional observations rather than a final Agency determination regarding your compliance. Your firm should submit a written response within fifteen business days.

Sincerely,

R. Delgado
Investigator
Office of Compliance, CDRH

To: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>; Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>
Date: Wed, 20 Feb 2019 14:22
Subject: RE: 55-degree wear retest results - concerning

Tom, Priya—

Looking at this from product management, altering the geometry now would have substantial downstream consequences. Apex has been positioned around stability, active patients, and “designed to last” performance. Revisiting the hardware would therefore change not only that narrative but also inventory, training, and the existing launch plan.

Could surgical-technique guidance provide a route before we pursue a redesign? If elevated inclination is the main concern, we might emphasize the target range through the surgical guide, lab training, and field education instead of modifying the cup itself. Tom, I recognize that this may not answer the engineering issue, but if the positioning relationship remains valid, it could serve as a suitable interim control.

I agree that this belongs on the agenda for the next design review, incorporating Meridian’s input and whatever Priya is able to retrieve from the Atlanta files. Until then, please keep the matter internal. We lack sufficient context for a broader message.

Carlos

-----Original Message-----
From: Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>
To: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Date: Wed, 13 Feb 2019 09:06
Subject: RE: 55-degree wear retest results - concerning

Tom—

The result merits further examination, but I would avoid describing it as indicative of field performance until the test condition is better understood.

DR-3 approved a wear-test protocol specifying 45° inclination, in line with practice at the time and the rationale documented in the DHF. Can you confirm whether 55° represents a plausible distribution of surgical positioning or instead a worst-case/outlier condition chosen to stress the construct? If we are evaluating a possible relationship to complaints, that distinction is important.

Before we escalate, please also involve Meridian Testing Labs so they can independently assess the setup, calculations, and interpretation. We should not overreact to a single retest until reproducibility and clinical relevance have been established.

I will examine TW-2019-0417, including the question of whether the Atlanta records contain implant-position information. The complaint file currently includes elevated metal ions and revision-related clinical notes, though I do not remember radiographic inclination being recorded consistently. Under the procedure, we can ask the reporting sites for any missing information.

Carlos, please refrain from external messaging until we have that further context.

Priya

Re: Voluntary Recall Notification - ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200 to V-2299
FDA Recall No. Z-1418-2022

Dear Sir or Madam:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is notifying the Food and Drug Administration that it is conducting a voluntary Class II recall involving specified lots of ApexHip acetabular cups. The devices subject to this action are ApexHip cobalt/chromium acetabular cups featuring KinetiCoat porous titanium coating and manufactured at Veridian’s Cork, Ireland facility.

This recall covers cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, produced between November 2021 and February 2022. Of the 1,140 units distributed in the United States, current lot-trace reconciliation indicates that 412 units have been implanted. The remaining units are in customer or distributor inventory, have been returned, or are still held in Veridian-controlled inventory while final reconciliation is pending.

The action began after two hospital customers submitted incoming-inspection reports, one of which involved Northgate Health System and another a hospital in the Denver area. Both reports described KinetiCoat flaking when the device was removed from its packaging. This recall does not include any other ApexHip lots.

Veridian’s investigation indicates that drift in plasma-spray parameters after a chamber maintenance event at the Cork facility is the probable root cause of the coating adhesion failures. Applicable batch records, chamber data, and maintenance documentation were reviewed and support this determination. The investigation is still ongoing, and Veridian will submit supplemental information if further findings change the scope or assessment of this action.

The immediate corrective measures are: (1) stopping distribution of the affected lots; (2) segregating affected product and reconciling inventory; (3) inspecting and requalifying the plasma-spray chamber; (4) confirming plasma-spray operating parameters and related monitoring controls; and (5) reviewing and revising maintenance and post-maintenance release procedures as appropriate. Routine production will not resume in the chamber until Quality has approved completion of the requalification requirements.

At the same time, customer notification letters are being issued to all known consignees. These letters direct recipients to identify, stop using, and return the affected product. Veridian will perform effectiveness checks and submit periodic status reports as required by FDA.

This action addresses coating adhesion and does not involve metal-ion wear or any other field performance concerns associated with ApexHip.

If you have questions, please contact me at (574) 555-0142 or dokonkwo@veridianortho.com.

Respectfully,

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
ENGINEERING MEMORANDUM

Date: March 10, 2022
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Subject: Explant analysis summary - Whitaker case, lot V-2114

Engineering’s visual and materials assessment of the retrieved ApexHip femoral head and acetabular cup from the revision performed by Dr. James Whitaker in Denver is summarized in this memo. Warsaw received the components on February 28, 2022, pursuant to return authorization RA-22-0317. The cup bears lot identification V-2114. Identifiers on the returned head agree with the operative record provided by Dr. Whitaker’s office.

According to the case materials, the revision followed persistent pain, increased serum cobalt and chromium levels, and imaging findings that the treating team characterized as concerning for an adverse local tissue reaction. The device examination does not constitute a clinical determination by me; that determination remains with the treating physician and Clinical/Quality. The findings that follow are restricted to the returned components and the associated debris sample.

Circumferential polishing was present on the femoral head bearing surfaces, while the most pronounced damage was concentrated in a band corresponding to the cup’s superior-lateral rim. On the cup bearing surface, directional wear striations run inward from the rim at approximately the 11 to 2 o’clock positions, using the surgeon’s orientation marks. A narrow region of matte discoloration and scratching is also present at the rim transition. This distribution does not match uniform, concentric articulation in the nominal orientation.

The postoperative radiograph available in the case file appears to show the cup positioned at a relatively high inclination angle. Clinical or the treating site should confirm the exact measurement; however, the apparent orientation falls within the range in which edge contact is more likely.

The pattern is materially similar to what we observed in the 2019 55-degree inclination reruns. In that testing, wear rose substantially after the contact patch shifted toward the cup rim, and the resulting head/cup surface damage was directional instead of evenly distributed. The retrieved surfaces in this case demonstrate the same fundamental mechanism: rim contact/edge loading followed by localized abrasive wear.

Analysis of the collected particulate residue found cobalt/chromium-containing debris. Digestion-sample quantitation measured 18.6 µg cobalt and 7.9 µg chromium per gram of recovered residue. Because of recovery limitations and handling during revision, these measurements should not be interpreted as a direct indication of total in vivo burden. Nevertheless, the composition and relative concentration are consistent with the elevated serum ion readings documented in the case materials.

The accessible KinetiCoat exterior surface showed no coating delamination. This case also does not appear connected to the Cork coating issue associated with the V-2200 series lots. V-2114 is outside that population.

In conclusion, the retrieval findings are consistent with the established edge-loading wear mechanism associated with high cup inclination, together with Co/Cr debris generation. Quality should include this case in the cumulative metal-ion complaint dataset and in the next MDR trending review. I recommend that the components and microscopy images remain with the complaint file. Engineering has retained the raw photos and measurement worksheet in the Apex retrieval folder.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip

MEMORANDUM

TO: Dana Okonkwo (VP, Regulatory Affairs), Rachel Steinberg (General Counsel), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (Chief Medical Officer), Marcus Lee (VP, Sales)
FROM: Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip)
DATE: September 28, 2021
SUBJECT: Draft "Dear Doctor" Letter – ApexHip Acetabular System Labeling Update

Based on the determinations made at our September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting, I have completed the first draft of the forthcoming customer communication ("Dear Doctor" letter) concerning the ApexHip Total Hip System.

The review team and executive leadership agreed that Veridian will continue active commercial distribution of ApexHip while immediately updating the Instructions for Use (IFU) labeling in response to emerging registry trends.

Background & Signal Summary
This communication is principally prompted by findings reported in the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 17th Annual Report. The report found a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip construct, versus an average class benchmark of approximately 3.2% among contemporary metal-on-metal (MoM) hip resurfacing and total replacement systems. Although internal clinical evaluations show that well-positioned constructs continue to achieve strong clinical survivorship, registry findings together with internal engineering assessments associate early revisions mainly with adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) related to elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels.

Proposed Letter Content & Labeling Guidance
The proposed notification focuses on patient safety, accurate surgical technique, and focused post-operative monitoring:

1. Patient Monitoring Recommendations: Clinicians should implement enhanced routine clinical and radiographic follow-up for every patient implanted with ApexHip, giving particular consideration to those who received larger femoral head diameters (≥44 mm). Routine cross-sectional imaging (MARS-MRI or ultrasound) and periodic whole blood cobalt and chromium metal-ion testing should be considered annually, or whenever a patient reports unexplained pain, clicking, or swelling.
2. Surgical Positioning & Angle Inclination: Revisions show a strong association with edge-loading phenomena. Under the updated labeling, surgeons are specifically directed to aim for an acetabular cup inclination angle of 40° to 45° and anteversion of 15° to 20°. Operating beyond these limits—particularly exceeding 50° of operative abduction—substantially raises the risk of accelerated fluid-film wear and premature component loosening.

Next Steps & Timeline
We are aiming to mail the notification in mid-October 2021 to all US and EU implanting orthopedic surgeons, chief medical officers, and relevant risk management personnel. Once the wording is finalized, reps will receive accompanying talking points.

Please examine the attached formal notification layout (`Apex_Dear_Doctor_Draft_v1.docx`) and return your redlines. Formal approval from Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and Clinical is required before Dana submits the final package to the agency and we move forward with mass distribution.

1. Purpose & Administrative Routing

This memorandum formally opens Claim Substantiation File CSF-2017-004 for every promotional asset that will support the commercial launch of the ApexHip Total Hip System at the April 2017 National Sales Kickoff in Dallas, Texas.

Under SOP-MKT-302 (*Promotional Material Review and Approval*), each item of collateral—including sales visual aids, detail sheets, patient education booklets, and digital properties administered through Kessler Reid—must link all explicit and implicit product-performance claims to verifiable engineering reports, clinical literature, or validated pre-clinical bench testing. Once finalized, the collateral will be recorded in the Agile PLM environment under change order ECO-2017-088.

2. General Regulatory Guidance

After discussions with Regulatory Affairs (D. Okonkwo), teams are reminded that FDA 510(k) clearance (K162447, issued March 9, 2017) establishes substantial equivalence to the predicate device (ClassicHip) solely for purposes of commercial distribution. Promotional language must never present the 510(k) clearance letter as affirmative clinical evidence of safety, superiority, or long-term therapeutic efficacy. Marketing agency partners and all field representatives are required to follow the cleared indications for use without deviation.

3. Promotional Claim Inventory and Substantiation Table

Claims identified in the primary launch brochure (P/N 093-4011) and the unbranded patient portal preview are listed below:

| Claim Text | Promotional Context | Primary Source Document | Review Status / Owner |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "Largest head diameter for stability" | Sales aid, HCP web banner (ApexHip head offerings: 36–50 mm vs. traditional 28–32 mm) | ApexHip Engineering Specifications (DHF Section 4.2, Drawing Series H-3xxx); ISO 14242 wear-testing inputs | Substantiated. Engineering sign-off complete (T. Halvorsen, 02/2017). Comparative jump-distance data validated. |
| "Durable bone ingrowth through advanced titanium plasma spray" | Surgical technique guide, acetabular detail sheet | KBT Due Diligence Technical Dossier (March 2016); KinetiCoat Porous Coating Adhesion & Shear Testing (Report TR-15-088) | Substantiated. Porosity and mean pore depth metrics verified against KBT acquisition transfer files. Owner: C. Mendes. |
| "Engineered for active adults seeking return to motion" | Patient brochures, "Active Life" print advertising | Demographics market research; cleared indications under K162447 (non-inflammatory degenerative joint disease) | Substantiated. Appropriate qualifier language embedded in fair balance section. Owner: A. Shah. |
| "Designed to last a lifetime of movement" | Launch brochure cover tagline, trade show display headers, introductory video | N/A (Internal promotional concept / aspirational) | FLAGGED / PENDING REVIEW. See Section 4 below. |

4. Substantiation Exceptions & Action Items

The statement *"designed to last a lifetime of movement"* has been identified for further review.

During cross-functional review, MarCom flagged the wording. Although it was intended as thematic, aspirational positioning for younger patient demographics (45–65 age bracket), the phrase implicitly suggests implant longevity and long-term survivorship. Veridian currently lacks prospective clinical revision-rate data, simulator wear data extending beyond 5 million standard cycles, and long-term registry tracking for the ApexHip construct; therefore, the company cannot substantiate an explicit assertion of lifetime durability.

The line remains on hold until clinical risk review is completed and Dr. Adeyemi provides explicit written sign-off. Should Medical Affairs determine that the wording creates excessive regulatory or compliance exposure, MarCom and Kessler Reid will revise the primary launch headline to either *"Engineered for a Lifetime of Movement"* or *"Designed for the Demands of Daily Movement,"* with suitable survivorship disclaimers.

Following up on our conversation, I updated the Apex model with September actuals and the latest field forecast. Its purpose is to frame revenue exposure through FY24; it does not seek to project either claim severity or claim timing.

Apex FY22 is currently projected to finish at approximately $71.0M, compared with the FY20 peak of $96.0M. Based on the underlying order data, the decline started before the June cup recall. |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| Label-driven decline | 71.0 | 54.7 | 45.9 | (35%) |
| Full market withdrawal | 71.0 | 48.3 | 42.6 | (40%) |

Under the status quo case, current labeling continues, no broad commercial action occurs, and modest attrition is offset by utilization in existing accounts. This most closely matches the current Sales operating plan, although I would not describe it as the base case with a high degree of confidence.

The label-driven decline case presumes an ongoing reduction in new implanters, decreased utilization at accounts that have placed Apex in a limited-use position, and growing price concessions when distributors attempt to preserve volume. Compared with the operating plan, this more closely represents the current path in the Southeast and certain Midwest accounts.

The withdrawal case presumes that, following an orderly market action, there are no new commercial placements, leaving only limited residual revenue from contracted inventory and replacement requirements. By necessity, this is a planning construct rather than a recommendation concerning product status.

For testing reserve adequacy, I recommend the full withdrawal scenario as the conservative revenue sensitivity. It leaves the least contribution available to absorb claims-related costs and does not depend on a recovery in surgeon confidence, which is absent from the current forecast submissions.

With respect to the voluntary Class II recall notice dated June 14, 2022, our hospital's central sterile and incoming inspection team placed multiple components in quarantine earlier this week. In particular, before the device reached the OR, an Apex acetabular cup from lot V-2247 was found inside its sterile blister pack with visible coating delamination. Inspection of the inner packaging showed the KinetiCoat porous surface actively shedding small particulate fragments.

An implant designed for immediate press-fit biological fixation cannot exhibit unassisted flaking during unwrapping; this is wholly unacceptable. Following your recall instructions, we returned six unopened units from this lot to our local distributor. I nevertheless require a specific explanation of what occurred in your plasma-spray process and how the lot was released.

1. Patient D.K. (DOB 11/14/1963): A primary left total hip was performed in March 2019 (Cup Lot V-1892, 54mm; Head Lot H-3112, 44mm). At 38 months post-op, the patient presented with groin pain and severe functional decline. Pre-op serum cobalt measured 9.4 ppb, while chromium measured 8.1 ppb. During revision on June 18, 2022, I found extensive metallosis, fluid-filled cystic collections, and abductor necrosis consistent with ARMD. Although the cup remained well-fixed, substantial edge-wear was evident on the bearing surface.

2. Patient R.M. (DOB 04/02/1958): The patient underwent a primary right total hip in August 2018 (Cup Lot V-1644, 52mm; Head Lot H-3088, 40mm) and was revised on June 27, 2022. A 6 cm pseudotumor was displacing the femoral neurovascular bundle. Explant examination showed gross blackened fluid and extensive destruction of soft tissue. Tissue samples confirmed severe histiocytic response and metal debris necrosis.

FROM: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer
DATE: October 26, 2021
SUBJECT: Preliminary Financial Exposure Note – Registry Signal Decision
CONFIDENTIAL / PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL WORK PRODUCT

After our conversation last week about the September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting, I requested Hannah Berg's assistance in developing a model of possible downstream exposure. Now that we have settled on continuing ApexHip commercial distribution, backed by a labeling revision and the forthcoming Dear Doctor advisory, we must define the financial boundaries if UK registry results (NJR) and domestic monitoring (AJRR) do not stabilize during the next 12 to 24 months.

This work is solely exploratory; it is not a formal accounting conclusion and does not constitute a GAAP accrual.

Scenario Modeling (FY 2022–2024 Outlook)

The forecast is driven chiefly by two factors: whether commercial volume continues and the realized cumulative revision gap relative to historical class baselines. With the present run-rate of approximately ~14,000 systems annually at an ASP of about ~$9,800, further movement toward the 7.1% 5-year revision rate identified by the NJR would create foreseeable indemnity and defense tailwinds.

| Scenario | Modeled Revision Uplift | Est. System Volume (3-Yr) | Potential Claims Exposure / Reserve Range |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Low Case | +1.5% to 2.0% over class average | 32,000 units (assumes tapering) | $8.0M – $11.5M |
| Mid Case | +3.0% to 3.5% over class average | 38,000 units (steady adoption) | $14.0M – $18.5M |
| High Case | +4.0%+ over class average | 42,000 units (aggressive growth) | $20.0M – $25.0M |

Under the *Low Case*, updates to our surgical technique labeling are assumed to become effective and reduce edge-loading outliers, leaving claims focused mainly on concentrated revisions and limited legal defense. The *High Case* assumes ongoing ARMD and ion-related complications result in formal litigation in multiple territories and require significant settlements on a per-case basis.

Recommendations

The requirements for an accrual under ASC 450 (Contingencies) are currently not satisfied. Given that no litigation has been actively filed and the causal relationship between technique and manufacturing remains uncertain, the loss is neither probable nor reasonably estimable.

1. Maintain Current Stance: Do not record a formal balance sheet reserve for Q3 or FY21 year-end.
2. Quarterly Registry Monitoring: Finance should obtain direct quarterly syntheses from Greg Novak's team so that NJR and AJRR curve inflections can be measured against these sensitivity bands.
3. Carrier Dialogue: Defer formal notifications to Aegis Specialty until Rachel's team finds a concrete filed claim that exceeds standard warranty resolutions.

Let's discuss this offline before preparing for the next Audit Committee meeting.

MEMORANDUM

Date: June 20, 2024
From: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer
Subject: End-of-Period Financial Summary - ApexHip Product Line Closure

This memorandum presents Finance’s current assessment of the ApexHip product line through June 30, 2024. It covers the line’s historical contribution, costs associated with its withdrawal, and the outlook for contingent liabilities. It is provided as a closing-period reference for ApexHip, while the related legal and claims matters remain unresolved.

Following 510(k) clearance, ApexHip entered the United States market in April 2017 and the European market in September 2017. Adoption was rapid within its targeted active-adult segment, and the product line became a significant contributor to Reconstructive revenue. Annual sales peaked in 2020, with approximately 14,200 systems producing approximately $96 million in revenue. That amount equaled roughly 22% of the Company’s consolidated revenue for the year.

Using booked sales through the withdrawal together with revenue that remains recognized, Finance estimates total ApexHip lifetime revenue for 2017 through 2024 at approximately $410 million. The estimate covers both U.S. and international sales and remains subject to ordinary quarter-end adjustments for revenue, returns, credits, and distributor true-ups. The voluntary market withdrawal on February 2, 2024 stopped new commercial sales, but certain customer credits issued after withdrawal, returns of field inventory, and service-related transactions are still being processed.

ApexHip’s financial consequences have emerged over multiple stages. In the third quarter of 2022, the Company established an $18 million reserve for Apex-related claims. That reserve was based on exposure that was known and reasonably estimable at the time, including pending claims activity, expected defense costs, and the information then available concerning product allegations. It was not intended to be a final projection of ultimate loss.

As further claims were brought and the federal proceeding progressed, Finance raised its internal range. Throughout 2023 and the first half of 2024, working estimates typically indicated potential Company-funded exposure of $45 million to $70 million. The range depended on assumptions about case inventory, dismissal rates, indemnity allocation, defense costs, insurance recoveries, and the timing and structure of a possible global resolution.

MDL 3102 now contains approximately 520 filed cases and continues to expand. Although the number of cases by itself does not establish ultimate liability, our reserve analyses have considered the filing rate, claimant medical profiles, revision status, and expenses associated with continuing coordinated litigation. Finance will keep working with Legal, Quality, Regulatory, and our outside advisors as additional information specific to individual cases becomes available.

For planning purposes, management is considering a proposed $80 million settlement contribution by Veridian, together with a tentative $40 million coverage contribution from Aegis Specialty. Both amounts remain subject to negotiation, policy analysis, allocation discussions, and agreement regarding a mediation framework. They do not constitute a completed settlement, a final coverage determination, or a fixed accounting conclusion. Aegis’s involvement is still tentative, and any recovery will depend on finalized terms and the applicable policy conditions.

Accordingly, ApexHip’s overall financial impact extends beyond the product-line reserve. It includes withdrawal expenses, customer credits, inventory-related charges, ongoing defense costs, and internal support expenses. Where practical, these items will continue to be monitored separately to prevent reserve changes from being combined with ordinary operational closeout costs.

Quarterly reserve reviews will continue through finalization of the mediation framework and resolution of all claims. Any material change to the anticipated Veridian contribution, Aegis participation, case inventory, or accounting treatment will be submitted through the standard quarter-end review process.

Owen Park
Chief Financial Officer

MEMORANDUM

Date: June 22, 2015
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
To: Priya Raman; Carlos Mendes
Subject: ApexHip concept design kickoff notes

Hello Priya and Carlos,

I am recording notes from last week’s concept kickoff to give us a baseline before the design inputs are finalized. This remains an early-stage effort, is progressing quickly, and should be expected to change.

The basic proposal is a total hip system with a Co/Cr femoral head and stem, using the same alloy family as ClassicHip and its established manufacturing route. These components would be paired with an acetabular cup featuring the new titanium porous coating obtained through the KBT deal. For the moment, I am referring to the coating internally as KinetiCoat, unless marketing prefers another name; Carlos, that decision is yours. The coating is the key differentiator: it should provide better bone ingrowth than our existing sintered bead surface. That improvement is the central justification for using metal-on-metal in this generation.

The current draft of the target design inputs is as follows:

- Head diameters will range from 36mm to 50mm in 2mm increments. The larger heads are intended to improve stability/ROM, which supports the selling point aimed at the "active" patient segment we continue to discuss.
- Cup sizes will extend from 44mm to 62mm, corresponding to the head range and including offset options.
- The wear-rate objective is to remain below the ClassicHip benchmark. We will obtain the actual value from the ClassicHip DHF; I believe Priya has that file. We need the polyethylene wear data as the comparator, even though this system will be MoM, because the failure mode is obviously different but leadership wants an apples-to-apples figure in the design-input document.
- The cup-placement inclination range has not yet been finalized. The current preference is to specify the standard 40-45 degree range on which surgeons are trained. I address this further below.

Open item — wear test protocol: no standard has been selected yet. ISO 14242 is the clear starting point because it is used universally and is the reference FDA will expect. The unresolved issue is whether to test at one inclination angle or conduct a matrix covering multiple angles to determine how cup positioning in the OR affects wear rate, given that surgeons do not consistently achieve the same angle. My preference is to include at least a sensitivity check, although doing so will increase the test campaign’s time and cost. Before taking this to DR-2, I would like Priya’s assessment from the quality/DHF perspective.

For the timeline, the goal is to complete and formally approve the design inputs by September 2015. This leaves time to reach DR-3 later this year for the wear-test-protocol decision and to begin finalizing the coating specification with the KBT engineers. Their due diligence notes indicated that they have limited long-term adhesion data, so our verification plan should address that rather than relying solely on their historical data.

Carlos, I need your perspective on the head/cup size matrix in relation to sales’ view of market demand, including whether 50mm heads would be excessive or instead provide a marketing advantage.

Let’s schedule 30 min next week to align before I prepare the formal write-up.

Post-Market Surveillance Memorandum

Date: June 5, 2023  
From: Greg Novak, Director, Post-Market Surveillance  
To: File  
Subject: Registry and complaint correlation memo - pre-MDL summary

This memorandum provides a consolidated account of how external registry results relate to Veridian’s internal ApexHip complaint and MDR trends through the current reporting period. I assembled it as a single reference because, as the pending state-court matters progress and may be coordinated, we should anticipate requests for this information.

In brief, the registry and complaint data have pointed in the same general direction since 2019. They are distinct datasets and cannot be substituted for one another, and neither independently establishes causation. Even so, both indicate earlier-than-expected revision among a subset of ApexHip patients, together with metal-ion findings, adverse local tissue reactions, and revision descriptions compatible with a wear-related mechanism.

1. Registry findings

The March 2021 UK National Joint Registry annual report recorded a five-year ApexHip revision rate of 7.1%, versus a 3.2% class average for the applicable total-hip population. NJR information has limitations: complete patient-level laboratory values are unavailable, surgeon technique variables are captured incompletely, and the product cohort is substantially smaller than the aggregate comparator group. Nevertheless, the difference’s direction and size justified the September 2021 Registry Signal Review.

AJRR extracts obtained in late 2021 likewise indicated that Apex had a higher revision signal than comparable contemporary total hips. At that point, the AJRR dataset was less mature than the NJR dataset, and its confidence intervals were broader. The mid-2022 AJRR refresh did not remove the signal; instead, it continued to indicate greater revision incidence for the Apex cohort, especially in cases coded using pain, metallosis/metal-debris terminology, instability, or aseptic loosening. Because coding practices differ among sites, these categories should not be regarded as clinical adjudications.

2. Internal complaints and MDRs

A material cluster first appeared in TrackWise complaint entries in 2018, including three metal-ion-related complaints involving Atlanta-area patients treated in Dr. Feld’s practice. During 2019, internal trend reports increasingly documented elevated cobalt and chromium, pain, fluid collections, tissue reaction, and early revision. Complete records or confirmed implant component details were not available for every reported case. Several cases were initially assigned broad pain or revision codes, with additional information received later through follow-up.

The MDR population has followed the same broad course. Reportable events rose as revisions and explant findings came in, but MDR timing should not be interpreted as the timing of the underlying event because of reporting lags, supplemental records, and follow-up. Accordingly, the internal complaint/MDR trend is most informative when examined by implant date and, where available, event date, rather than by filing date alone.

3. Mechanism assessment

This pattern accords with the edge-loading wear mechanism that Tom Halvorsen’s engineering team identified in its 2019 re-analysis of Apex wear testing. With cup inclination at 55 degrees, testing demonstrated approximately four- to six-fold greater wear than under the standard 45-degree protocol. The clinical and registry information does not establish cup inclination for every affected patient, and patient, surgical, and implant factors may also play a role. Nonetheless, elevated Co/Cr results and ARMD-type findings in the complaint records are directionally consistent both with the engineering explanation and with the registry revision signal.

This assessment is distinct from the 2022 KinetiCoat cup-lot recall. Lots V-2200 through V-2299 were recalled for coating adhesion and a manufacturing parameter drift at Cork; without a case-specific basis, they should not be analytically combined with the metal-ion/wear signal.

Recommendation: Quality and PMS should complete the Apex complaint database, including the current reconciliation of duplicate and follow-up records, and preserve a cross-reference linking complaint/MDR records to the relevant NJR and AJRR citations. Any response provided externally should expressly describe data-source limitations and reporting lags, and should distinguish the coating recall from the wear-related issue.

FROM: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip

SUBJECT: Rationale and Drafting for Proposed Revision to ApexHip System Instructions for Use (IFU)

This memorandum follows the consensus reached at the September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting and sets out the commercial and clinical rationale for proposed changes to the ApexHip Acetabular Cup Instructions for Use (IFU-0144, Rev. D), together with revisions to the related Surgical Technique Guide.

1. Strategic Context & Objective

Recent registry publications, especially the 2021 NJR Annual Report reporting a 7.1% cumulative revision rate at 5 years, make it necessary for the manufacturer to implement clear risk-mitigation measures. Nevertheless, as reviewed with senior leadership, our aim is to give operating surgeons practical clinical guidance that reflects these registry trends without issuing an overly broad safety communication or taking market action that might unintentionally weaken commercial confidence in the Apex platform.

Presenting wear performance in relation to stringent anatomical placement requirements allows us to promote optimal surgical execution and respond to the underlying registry signal without creating wider market concern.

2. Proposed IFU Revisions (Section 4: Warnings and Precautions)

We recommend inserting the following wording into Section 4.2 (*Implant Positioning and Wear Performance*):

> *"CAUTION: Clinical outcomes and bearing couple wear characteristics are highly sensitive to acetabular component orientation. Internal bench testing demonstrates that cup abduction (inclination) angles exceeding 45 degrees, particularly when combined with excessive anteversion, lead to localized edge-loading and significantly accelerated volumetric wear rates. Surgeons should verify intraoperative cup orientation using radiographic or navigational alignment aids to maintain an inclination target of 40° to 45°."*

Drafting Note: Although the proposed wording expressly reflects our internal bench-testing results concerning high-angle biomechanics, it deliberately presents the issue as an opportunity to optimize operative technique rather than as an intrinsic product limitation.

3. Surgical Technique Guide Additions

At the same time, we will release an addendum to the ApexHip Surgical Technique Guide that highlights:
- Confirmation of the "safe zone" (Lewinnek criteria) before final cup impaction.
- Particular cautions concerning variations in patient anatomy, including pelvic tilt during high-flexion activities, which may artificially increase the functional inclination angle beyond 45°.

4. Alignment with Planned Communications

The revised labeling will provide the technical basis for the "Dear Healthcare Provider" letter planned for release in mid-October 2021. By stating that increased wear is primarily associated with component positioning outside the validated envelope, the communication appropriately directs attention toward surgical precision and patient selection.

5. Next Steps and Action Required

In accordance with design change procedures, this revision will be submitted through an expedited Change Order in Agile.

Dana — please provide your formal regulatory sign-off on the language proposed above by Friday, September 24, enabling Marketing and Regulatory to complete the October Dear Doctor communication draft and verify filing requirements under 21 CFR 803 / 820 before distribution.

All,

Please review the attached draft of ECO-2019-118 before I submit it to the change control board. It follows up on the 55-degree wear re-test circulated in Feb (Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx). The 4-6x wear multiplier observed at high inclination is caused by edge contact at the cup rim rather than a bulk material problem, which means the corrective action is geometric.

The draft ECO proposes the following:

1. Make the cup-rim chamfer angle smaller, creating a shallower transition than the current spec. The draft identifies a target, but I would like Meridian's input before finalizing the number.
2. Modify the KinetiCoat application boundary by moving it back from the rim edge, avoiding coating directly up to the contact zone. This should also provide a secondary benefit by improving the adhesion margin.
3. Conduct another test series at Meridian at both 45 deg (baseline, per our current protocol) and 55 deg. This will give us apples to apples data on the revised geometry before we commit to tooling.

The preliminary cost is $340k for new tooling and re-validation testing. End-to-end timing is approximately 9 months, with tooling lead time as the long pole; the testing portion should take maybe 10-12 weeks.

Meeting Date: December 14, 2020
Location: Warsaw, IN — Engineering Conference Room B / Teams
Minutes prepared by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs)

1. Purpose
The meeting was convened to re-evaluate ECO-2019-118, concerning the proposed cup/liner geometry modification intended to address edge-loading wear observed during 2019 testing at 55° inclination. The change had originally been deferred during the 2019 DR review. The reassessment was prompted by updated complaint-trend information.

2. Discussion

2.1 Complaint trend data. Raman reviewed updated TrackWise trend information. It indicates that metal-ion-related complaints have continued to rise gradually since the 2018 Atlanta cluster, with further isolated reports recorded through Q3 2020 from the Denver and Nashville territories. Raman stated that, under the current procedure, the trend remains within historical variability, while also acknowledging that its slope has not flattened.

2.2 Wear test results. Halvorsen revisited the 2019 55° inclination re-test results, first reported in the Feb 2019 memo to Raman/Mendes. Those results demonstrated 4–6x greater wear at the higher cup inclination angles than under the standard 45° protocol used for 510(k) clearance. No additional bench testing has taken place since then, and the referenced data remain unchanged from 2019.

2.3 Cost of implementation. Halvorsen provided a revised estimate for carrying out the proposed liner geometry modification. The 2019 estimate had been approximately $260,000. Since then, tooling at the Cork facility has changed because new fixturing was installed for an unrelated coating process change. As a result, the present estimate is approximately $410,000, primarily due to re-tooling and requalification of the injection/machining tooling.

2.4 Registry data. Okonkwo reported that the NJR annual report addressing ApexHip's 5-year outcomes is anticipated in early 2021 and will contain updated revision-rate information pertinent to the decision. Mendes concurred that the report would materially affect messaging and design prioritization.

3. Resolutions

3.1 ECO-2019-118 is deferred once more. The team determined that proceeding with the design change now is not justified because (a) complaint trend data continues to fall within procedural thresholds, (b) implementation would cost $410,000, and (c) NJR registry data is expected in Q1 2021 and should clarify the scope and urgency of any design action.

3.2 After the NJR report is received, the team will reconvene promptly and reconsider ECO-2019-118 using the new data.

4. Action Items
- Upon receipt, Okonkwo will circulate the NJR report (Owner: Okonkwo)

Post-Market Surveillance — Interim Report

Report No.: PMS-2021-014
Date: June 28, 2021
Prepared by: Greg Novak, Director, Post-Market Surveillance
Product: ApexHip Total Hip System (all cup/head/stem configurations)
Distribution: Quality, Regulatory Affairs, R&D, Clinical Affairs (internal working file, pre-decision)

1. Purpose

This interim report reviews post-market complaint trends involving ApexHip metal-ion and wear-related events together with external registry information from the UK National Joint Registry (NJR) and preliminary American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) figures. Its purpose is to support a cross-functional determination of the appropriate next steps.

2. Complaint Trend Summary

TrackWise complaints classified under metal-ion elevation, ARMD, pseudotumor, or related revision-for-wear categories have continued to rise since 2019. Compared with the 2019 baseline, annual complaint volume for this category increased by approximately 85% in 2020, and the annualized figure through Q1 2021 continues along the same path. The increase cannot be attributed solely to higher implant volume: when normalized to units sold, the rate per 1,000 implants is likewise increasing rather than remaining flat. I want to be cautious in interpreting this result because TrackWise coding practices changed to some extent during 2020 (see Raman's Q4 2020 coding audit), potentially explaining part of the observed rise. Nevertheless, even after applying a conservative adjustment, a genuine upward signal remains.

3. Registry Correlation

According to the March 2021 NJR annual report, ApexHip's 5-year revision rate was 7.1%, compared with a 3.2% class average for all MoM and non-MoM large-head hip systems combined. The ApexHip rate is therefore more than twice the comparator. I compared the NJR cohort dates with our launch and complaint timelines, and registry data begins to show the divergence at approximately 3 years post-launch. That timing is reasonably consistent with the expected clinical appearance of edge-loading wear effects if Halvorsen's 2019 high-inclination wear-test findings apply in the field (see his Feb 2019 memo to Raman/Mendes re: 55° inclination testing, 4-6x wear vs. the 45°-only protocol used for original clearance).

AJRR information remains preliminary because only partial 2021 reporting is available, but the initial results indicate a comparable directional pattern across large-head MoM configurations generally, including ApexHip. At this point, I would regard the AJRR figures as corroborative, not definitive; limitations include sample size and reporting lag. I will provide a more complete AJRR analysis in the Q3 update.

4. Assessment

In combination, internal complaint trends, NJR results, and preliminary AJRR data now provide three independent signals pointing in the same direction. Each source has individual limitations—coding changes, reliance on a single registry, or immature data—but, in my view, the agreement among all three is unlikely to be coincidental.

I also want to note that ECO-2019-118—the design modification proposed by Halvorsen's team after the 2019 re-testing and deferred at that time—has not been reconsidered. In light of the registry relationship described above, I believe it is appropriate to reopen that decision rather than regard it as resolved.

5. Recommendation

I recommend that the cross-functional group comprising Regulatory, Quality, Clinical, R&D, and Marketing meet formally in Q3 to conduct a full review of this data package and decide whether labeling revisions, a surgeon communication, or a design/manufacturing action is warranted. Considering the direction of both the complaint information and the registry signal, I do not believe this review should be postponed until the year-end review. I am willing to present the complete data set. If useful for the discussion, I can also prepare a more detailed analysis by cup inclination angle using surgeon-reported operative notes, although compiling that information will require a couple weeks.

Attachments: NJR_2021_Apex_extract.xlsx, TrackWise_MoM_trend_2019-2021.xlsx

— Greg Novak
Director, Post-Market Surveillance

ENGINEERING MEMORANDUM

Date: March 22, 2021
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
To: KneeFlex Design History File
Subject: Summary of KneeFlex Design Change ECO-2021-044

ECO-2021-044 recommends modifying the porous-coating application process for the KneeFlex tibial baseplate. The purpose is to improve manufacturing yield. The change will not affect the finished device’s intended use, material specification, implant geometry, packaging configuration, sterilization method, or performance requirements.

1. Background and rationale

Since January, the Warsaw manufacturing facility has experienced inconsistent yield in the tibial-baseplate coating cell. The main causes have been visual-inspection rejects for incomplete posterior-edge coverage and variable surface appearance in the medial corner. The existing method uses a fixed fixture angle and applies the coating in one pass. Batch-record review and observations on the production line indicate that the part’s orientation during the last portion of that pass is contributing to uneven deposition.

Under ECO-2021-044, the fixture orientation will be adjusted by 12 degrees, and the existing single-pass method will be replaced by two controlled passes. These settings are intended to make coverage more consistent and decrease rework and scrap while leaving the released coating specification unchanged. The acceptance criteria will remain those already specified in KF-WI-217 and the KneeFlex tibial baseplate drawing package.

This action is not being initiated because of a field complaint trend. No clinical or product-performance issue has been identified in connection with the current process. The objective is instead to increase manufacturing yield and eliminate avoidable inspection rejects.

2. Proposed verification plan

Engineering will produce three pilot lots with the modified fixture orientation and application sequence. These will be evaluated against three recent production lots made with the current process. The testing will consist of:

- Measuring coating thickness at the standard mapped locations, including the posterior and medial-edge locations;
- Performing visual coverage inspection in accordance with KF-WI-217;
- Conducting adhesion tests on representative coupons and baseplate samples;
- Verifying surface roughness;
- Inspecting finished-baseplate dimensions after coating; and
- Reviewing process capability for coating thickness and the visual-inspection reject rate.

Sample quantities will be established in the verification protocol before testing begins. Implementation will be halted if any result falls outside the currently released acceptance criteria, pending Design Assurance review. Manufacturing Engineering will additionally verify that the modified fixture can be cleaned and maintained using the existing work instructions.

Because the device design and coating requirements remain unchanged, no new clinical evaluation is proposed. Regulatory Affairs will review the completed verification package and record the rationale for deciding whether a new submission is necessary. The current assessment is that the change is a manufacturing-process modification within the established design envelope.

3. DHF and controlled-document updates

The following records must be completed or updated before release:

- ECO-2021-044 approval record and implementation checklist;
- Process FMEA revised to identify the changed orientation and two-pass sequence;
- Manufacturing work instruction and fixture setup sheet revised;
- Verification protocol and report;
- Training records for coating-cell operators and inspectors;
- Process validation summary updated, if the pilot data require it; and
- DHF index entry connecting the ECO, risk assessment, test report, and released work instructions.

The change-control package must state that the reason for the change is yield improvement. It must not describe current production material as nonconforming unless that material failed the existing release criteria.

To maintain process consistency, the change-control package uses the same template as prior ApexHip ECOs. This reference concerns document format only; it does not indicate an ApexHip technical evaluation or a shared design issue.

I will distribute the draft verification protocol by Friday. Manufacturing must reserve the coating cell for the pilot run before the April preventive-maintenance window.

Tom

MEETING MINUTES

Registry Signal Review Meeting
Date: September 14, 2021
Time: 9:00–10:00 AM
Location: The Hub — Reserve B
Prepared by: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs

Attendees: Dana Okonkwo; Greg Novak; Priya Raman; Dr. Leon Adeyemi; Carlos Mendes; Marcus Lee; Rachel Steinberg
By phone: Rob Castellano, CEO

Purpose
The meeting was held to assess the current ApexHip registry signal and decide whether continued commercialization, accompanied by further risk mitigation, is still appropriate.

Discussion

1. Registry data. Greg Novak presented data from the March 2021 NJR annual report. ApexHip’s reported five-year revision rate stands at 7.1%, versus a 3.2% average for the class. The disparity persists following the available review of age and head-size strata, though the registry cannot fully adjust for surgeon technique, patient selection, or cup position.

Greg additionally examined the latest AJRR extracts. Although the AJRR population has a shorter follow-up period than the NJR cohort, it shows the same general pattern: early revisions are trending upward, with reported indications including elevated metal ions, ARMD, unexplained pain, and loosening. Greg identified limitations in both indication coding and data completeness. He advised monthly monitoring through the next formal registry refresh.

2. Clinical interpretation. Dr. Adeyemi said the signal is concerning and requires active mitigation. In his view, the registry information currently available does not by itself demonstrate a design defect or justify an immediate determination that every ApexHip recipient has the same degree of risk. He pointed out that cup inclination, patient activity, and other clinical factors could affect metal-on-metal wear and revision risk. He recommended more intensive monitoring, improved surgeon direction regarding patient selection and surgical technique, and rapid assessment of new clinical information instead of immediate withdrawal from the market.

3. Regulatory and complaint considerations. Dana Okonkwo discussed the continuing obligation to assess reportability and trend information under 21 CFR 803. Priya Raman confirmed that complaints concerning elevated cobalt/chromium levels, ARMD, pseudotumor findings, unexplained pain, and revisions are being entered into and evaluated in TrackWise in accordance with procedure. Dana stressed that complaint trending, MDR determinations, and registry surveillance must stay coordinated and be documented contemporaneously.

4. Commercial and communications considerations. Carlos Mendes and Marcus Lee considered the operational consequences of withdrawing ApexHip compared with issuing revised labeling and field communications. Marcus said that, if ApexHip remains available, the sales organization will need clear, controlled instructions. Rachel Steinberg asked that external communications accurately represent the available data and avoid describing the registry findings as conclusive.

Decision

The group decided that ApexHip sales would continue at this time, provided the following risk-mitigation actions are taken:

• Update the labeling to stress appropriate surgical technique, including cup inclination angle, patient selection, and clinical follow-up considerations.
• Develop a Dear Doctor letter for distribution to implanting surgeons in October 2021.
• Expand monitoring of post-market complaints and registry trends.

Rob Castellano joined the decision discussion by phone and agreed with this approach.

Action Items

1. Carlos Mendes: Work with Regulatory, Clinical, and Marketing to coordinate the proposed ApexHip labeling changes. Initial draft due September 24.
2. Devon Mitchell: Draft the Dear Doctor letter for review by Regulatory and Legal. Initial draft due September 27.
3. Priya Raman: Put enhanced complaint-trend monitoring in place and send Regulatory and PMS a monthly summary beginning October 2021.
4. Greg Novak: Maintain monthly NJR/AJRR surveillance and promptly escalate material changes.
5. Dana Okonkwo: Verify the regulatory documentation and review requirements applicable to the labeling update and surgeon communication.

Dana

This memo records the Performance Improvement Plan for Denise Ferro, which takes effect August 2, 2021. Priya Raman and HR jointly developed it in response to performance issues found while preparing for the June 2021 FDA inspection of the Warsaw facility. During the preceding quarter, Ms. Ferro's queue had a median time-to-decision of 14 business days, while multiple files remained open for more than 45 days without documented justification. If the metrics listed above are not achieved by the end of the 60-day period, or if another late MDR determination occurs during the plan period, further disciplinary action may be taken, up to and including termination of employment, in accordance with Veridian's performance management policy.

Re: Status Update on Recall – Z-1418-2022, ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200 through V-2299

Dear Sir or Madam:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is providing this periodic update on its voluntary Class II recall involving designated ApexHip acetabular cup lots, FDA Recall Number Z-1418-2022. Initiated on June 14, 2022, the recall followed reports that KinetiCoat coating had flaked during incoming inspection and product preparation.

The products involved are ApexHip acetabular cups produced at Veridian’s Cork, Ireland facility from November 2021 through February 2022. The affected lot numbers are V-2200 through V-2299.

Veridian’s distribution and reconciliation records, current as of July 22, 2022, show the following:

| Category | Units |
|---|---:|
| Total units distributed | 1,140 |
| Units reported implanted | 412 |
| Remaining units subject to retrieval | 728 |
| Remaining units retrieved to date | 728 |

Every known non-implanted unit from the affected lot range has been identified and recovered from domestic consignee inventory. Veridian is continuing effectiveness checks with customers and distributors to verify that the recall notification was received and that inventory reconciliation has been completed.

The investigation determined that plasma-spray parameter drift after a chamber maintenance event caused the adhesion deficiency. This condition impacted the process used to apply the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating and could lead to insufficient coating adhesion.

Corrective measures are now in place at the Cork facility. Veridian has specifically introduced a corrective maintenance verification protocol that requires documented confirmation of plasma-spray operating parameters after chamber maintenance and before product is released for routine production. This protocol provides for enhanced process verification, examination of chamber settings, and Quality approval before manufacturing resumes.

Veridian will keep assessing recall effectiveness and monitoring customer responses. Another status report will be submitted within 30 days.

Should the Agency need further information, please contact me.

Internal Memorandum

Date: February 11, 2019  
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip  
To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling  
Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip  
Subject: ApexHip wear re-test results at 55 degree inclination

Hello Priya and Carlos,

I wanted to bring this to your attention before proceeding further, because I am not comfortable with the results I am seeing.

At DR-3 in 2016, we finalized the wear-test protocol at 45 degrees inclination only, in accordance with ISO 14242, and that protocol has remained in the DHF ever since. Since last fall, I have suspected that we should also evaluate off-nominal cup positioning, as that more closely reflects what occurs in many actual hips depending on surgical technique. Accordingly, I asked Meridian Labs to repeat the protocol at 55 degrees cup inclination using a new set of cup/head pairs from the same lot family as production and with the same head material (Co/Cr on Co/Cr).

The results are available in Meridian report MTL-19-0142, dated 2/6/19. The raw figures are:

- At 45° inclination (the standard angle corresponding to our cleared data): approximately 2.1 mm3 per million cycles volumetric wear, consistent with the data submitted in the 510(k).
- At 55° inclination: approximately 9.8–12.4 mm3 per million cycles, depending on the sample. This is 4 to 6x the standard-angle result.

The difference is substantial. At 55°, the cup-rim wear scar has precisely the edge-loading pattern I identified in my 2015 concept-phase notes, when we were still establishing head/cup clearance tolerances. I had predicted that high inclination could produce this outcome, but we did not include it in the formal test matrix because ISO 14242 does not require it and DR-3 concluded that the standard angle was adequate for clearance purposes. In retrospect, I believe that decision was either incorrect or incomplete.

Because this is a MoM system, the debris is not solely a mechanical concern; it also involves Co/Cr ion generation. Greater wear volume at increased inclination will mean greater ion release in patients whose cups are positioned steeply, whether that results from surgical variability or from cup-design geometry that does not tolerate the positioning well.

Priya — has TrackWise identified anything that might correspond with these findings? I am considering the Atlanta cluster from last August, involving three patients from Feld's practice. I cannot see the implant positioning information for those cases, but if any involved high-inclination placement, the relationship could be more than coincidental.

I want to proceed cautiously: this is a single laboratory run with a small sample, and I have not yet completed the statistical analysis. I need to examine variance across the sample set before making any definitive statement. However, the size of the difference is sufficient that I believe we should seriously begin evaluating either a change to the cup geometry (greater clearance-angle tolerance, perhaps with a modified rim profile) or different head material/size combinations to lessen sensitivity to edge loading.

Could we schedule 20 minutes this week to review the next steps? I would prefer that we address this proactively rather than have it surface through another channel.

Best,  
Tom

MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: Q4 2021 Quarterly Registry Review Update  
Date: January 10, 2022  
Time: 10:00–11:00 AM ET  
Location: Hub, Conference Room 2B / Teams hybrid  
Minutes prepared by: Devon Mitchell

Attendees: Greg Novak (Post-Market Surveillance), Dana Okonkwo (Regulatory Affairs), Priya Raman (Quality & Complaint Handling), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (CMO)

1. Purpose  
The scheduled follow-up to the September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review was held to determine whether more recent registry information alters the assessment that supported continuing sales of ApexHip with the labeling update and October 2021 Dear Doctor letter.

2. AJRR Q4 2021 Data (Novak)  
Novak reviewed the AJRR figures from late 2021. ApexHip revision rates continue to exceed the broader class average, matching the direction and magnitude of the March 2021 NJR result, which showed a 7.1% five-year revision rate compared with a 3.2% class average. He explained that AJRR covers a shorter follow-up period than NJR, while also observing that its quarter-over-quarter trend line is not improving. Novak advised caution in interpreting one quarter in isolation, but said that two successive registries are now indicating the same pattern.

3. Discussion — Is the Current Response Sufficient?  
Okonkwo questioned whether, in light of the AJRR confirmation, the label update and surgeon letter are sufficient, or whether the company should reconsider a design modification, referring to the ECO-2019-118 proposal deferred in 2019, or impose a temporary sales pause while additional analysis is conducted.

Raman reported that TrackWise complaint volumes have not exhibited a corresponding increase since distribution of the Dear Doctor letter. She nevertheless acknowledged that this may indicate underreporting or a delay rather than resolution of the issue.

Adeyemi said the registry signal is clinically concerning, but the relative contributions of surgical technique, including inclination angle, and device design have not been definitively distinguished. He added that a sales pause would be a substantial measure and should not be based solely on registry data without additional correlation to wear testing.

The group also generally discussed the anticipated litigation hold, which is expected to be entered February 1, 2022, after Whitfield & Barr's engagement in January. Everyone agreed that this makes it more important to demonstrate active company monitoring and reassessment, but did not consider it a change to the substantive risk analysis.

4. Decision

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
ENGINEERING TEST SUMMARY REPORT

Date: 18 April 2019
Prepared by: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
Product: KneeFlex Total Knee System
Subject: Summary of Meridian Testing Labs’ KneeFlex Wear Report

Purpose

The purpose of this report is to present the final findings from Meridian Testing Labs’ simulator wear assessment of the KneeFlex tibial insert. The evaluation followed the ISO 14243 knee wear simulation protocol for five million cycles. The tested component was the production-intent UHMWPE tibial insert used with the standard KneeFlex cobalt-chromium femoral component.

In summary, the wear results matched expectations. No test station exhibited an outlier pattern warranting investigation of the design or material.

Test Configuration

Six stations were evaluated by Meridian with 10 mm medium congruent KneeFlex tibial inserts. These were gamma-sterilized, production-equivalent packaged parts from the 2018 pilot build. Standard polished Co/Cr femoral components were used. The lubricant was bovine serum at the protocol-specified concentration, with periodic changes and soak controls to correct for fluid uptake.

ISO 14243 loading and motion conditions were used. Inspections and gravimetric measurements occurred at intervals of one million cycles. At every pull point, Meridian also visually examined the articular surfaces.

Results

The corrected wear volumes after five million cycles are listed below.

| Test Station | Tibial Insert Size | Wear Volume at 5M Cycles (mm³) | Average Wear Rate (mm³/MC) | Observations |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 10 mm Medium | 37.8 | 7.6 | Uniform polish, no delamination |
| 2 | 10 mm Medium | 41.2 | 8.2 | Minor medial polish |
| 3 | 10 mm Medium | 39.6 | 7.9 | No unusual surface findings |
| 4 | 10 mm Medium | 43.1 | 8.6 | Light anterior contact polish |
| 5 | 10 mm Medium | 38.9 | 7.8 | No unusual surface findings |
| 6 | 10 mm Medium | 40.5 | 8.1 | Uniform polish, no delamination |

At five million cycles, the mean corrected wear volume was 40.2 mm³. Values across stations ranged from 37.8 to 43.1 mm³, and the mean calculated wear rate was 8.0 mm³ per million cycles.

Control specimens behaved as anticipated with respect to fluid uptake. Before issuing the final values shown above, Meridian incorporated the soak-control correction. The raw mass-loss results and control information remain available in Meridian report MTL-KF-19-044 and its accompanying electronic worksheet.

Surface Findings

No test insert showed cracking, pitting, delamination, or gross material loss during visual examination. Medial and lateral bearing surfaces displayed the expected polished contact regions. Station 4 showed somewhat more visible anterior polish than the remaining stations; however, its gravimetric result was still within the total range, and no related damage pattern was observed.

Meridian reported no mechanical interruptions, fixture failures, or protocol deviations during the five-million-cycle test.

Conclusion

Under the tested ISO 14243 simulator conditions, the KneeFlex tibial insert achieved acceptable wear performance through five million cycles. The results were consistent among all six stations and support continued use of the existing insert geometry and material specification.

Meridian’s final signed report, MTL-KF-19-044, together with the station-level measurement workbook, has been filed in the KneeFlex design verification folder. Based solely on these findings, no further simulator testing is recommended.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
CHANGE CONTROL BOARD — MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: Review of ECO-2019-118 (ApexHip Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry)
Date: April 2, 2019
Time: 10:00–11:15 AM
Location: Warsaw HQ, Building 2, Engineering Conference Room
Recorded by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip), Devon Mitchell (Sr. Regulatory Specialist), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs)

1. Background
Halvorsen reviewed the February 2019 re-analysis of the wear testing, which indicated wear rates 4–6x higher at a 55-degree cup inclination than at the 45-degree standard applied in the original ISO 14242 protocol (DR-3, Nov 2016). ECO-2019-118 was initiated to assess a proposed alteration to the rim geometry aimed at decreasing edge-loading wear at greater inclination angles.

2. Discussion
The Meridian Labs results supporting the increased wear were outlined by Halvorsen. He explained that implementing the change would involve re-tooling the cup mold and conducting another series of bench tests, with an estimated duration of 4–6 months and approximately $650K in NRE. Mitchell asked whether the modification would necessitate a new 510(k) or could instead be addressed through a letter-to-file determination. Okonkwo responded that, because of its potential effect on predicate equivalence, a geometry change of this type would likely require a new submission and would introduce regulatory timeline risk.

Raman stated that the current TrackWise complaint volume involving metal-ion-related issues remained low, consisting of a single-digit cluster from the 2018 Atlanta group (TW-2018-0912 et seq.), and that no definite domestic registry signal had appeared. Mendes expressed commercial concern that the "Active Life" launch momentum could be disrupted and questioned whether the wear results represented real-world inclination angles or only worst-case bench conditions. Halvorsen confirmed that the bench testing used a fixed 55-degree angle selected to stress edge loading, while clinical inclination distribution data was still unavailable.

The participants considered the cost, regulatory burden, and lack of a confirmed clinical signal at this time as reasons not to implement an immediate design change.

3. Resolution
The Change Control Board voted to DEFER ECO-2019-118. In the board’s assessment, the clinical signal and complaint trend evidence were insufficient at this time to support accepting the cost and regulatory risk associated with the proposed rim geometry modification. The decision will be reconsidered after additional wear data and updated complaint trending are received.

Vote: 4 in favor of deferral (Raman, Mendes, Mitchell, Okonkwo), 1 opposed (Halvorsen), recommending continued monitoring.

4. Action Items
- Raman will prepare a quarterly summary of complaint trends for ApexHip metal-ion/wear-related events, due end of Q2 2019.
- Halvorsen will proceed with informal wear testing at varied inclination angles outside the formal ECO scope and present the results at the next review.
- Mitchell will record the rationale for deferral in the DHF change log for ECO-2019-118.
- The next review will be scheduled after updated data is received, no later than Q4 2019.

The attendees present approved the minutes by consensus.
