MEMORANDUM

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. — Quality Assurance

Date: August 15, 2019  
From: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling  
To: File / Distribution per QA-SOP-014  
Re: ApexHip, Q2 2019 Quarterly Complaint Trending Summary

Purpose

The purpose of this memorandum is to present the ApexHip complaint-trending results for Q2 2019 (April–June), in accordance with QA-SOP-014 (Complaint Trending and Analysis).

Summary of Complaint Volume

During Q2 2019, TrackWise recorded 11 complaints concerning ApexHip, an increase from the 8 recorded in Q1 2019. Seven of those complaints described elevated metal ion (Co/Cr) levels and/or early revision surgery, versus 5 comparable complaints in Q1 2019. Metal-ion-related complaints have therefore continued to rise across the last two quarters.

Complaints by region (metal-ion/revision subset, n=7):

| Region | Count |
|---|---|
| Southeast | 6 |
| Northeast | 2 |
| Midwest | 3 |

(Note: the table totals 11 because it shows the overall regional distribution for all Q2 complaints rather than only the metal-ion subset; the Southeast count includes 4 metal-ion-related cases.)

Review of the records indicates that most affected implants are associated with index surgeries conducted in 2017–2018, matching the pattern seen in prior quarters. The surgeon of record was established for every case. Although no individual implanting surgeon represents a disproportionate share this quarter, the Southeast remains the largest single source, consistent with Dr. Feld's practice volume in that territory.

MDR Assessment

The complaints were assessed separately against the reportability criteria in 21 CFR 803.50. Under the applicable procedure, none of the seven metal-ion/revision complaints, considered on its own, reaches the mandatory-reporting threshold. Based on the clinical documentation currently available, no complaint describes a malfunction likely to cause or contribute to death or serious injury if it recurred. The individual decisions are recorded in the corresponding TrackWise files (TW-2019-0398 through TW-2019-0441, non-consecutive).

Trend Assessment and Recommendation

Although no individual complaint independently creates an MDR obligation, the increase from 5 to 7 quarter over quarter in the metal-ion/revision category is significant. Under QA-SOP-014 Section 6.2, this warrants continued close observation as Q3 begins. I recommend flagging the trend for consideration of a formal CAPA because the pattern is consistent across regions and the affected units are concentrated in the 2017–2018 surgical cohort.

I further recommend working with Design Engineering (Tom Halvorsen) to review the wear-testing results obtained at 55-degree cup inclination earlier this year. Several revision cases mention elevated inclination angles documented intraoperatively. A joint assessment could help determine whether device-related factors are contributing to the trend or whether the findings remain within expected variation for the surgical population.

This summary will be sent to Regulatory Affairs (D. Okonkwo) for awareness and to Post-Market Surveillance (G. Novak) for incorporation into the next registry data comparison.

Priya Raman  
Director, Quality & Complaint Handling

Regulatory Affairs Memorandum

Date: November 15, 2022
From: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs
Subject: Recall Closure Memorandum - Z-1418-2022, ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200-V-2299

This memorandum records the completed reconciliation and recommends closing Veridian Orthopedics’ voluntary Class II recall involving ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299 (FDA Recall No. Z-1418-2022).

Veridian initiated the recall on June 14, 2022, after two hospital incoming-inspection locations reported KinetiCoat coating flaking on cups taken from sterile packaging. The affected lots were produced at the Cork facility between November 2021 and February 2022. The field action was restricted to the specified acetabular cup lots and did not relate to post-market reports involving metal ion levels, wear, or ARMD.

The final distribution reconciliation is shown below:

| Disposition | Units |
|---|---:|
| Total units distributed | 1,140 |
| Confirmed implanted before recall notification | 412 |
| Returned to Veridian / distributor inventory | 681 |
| Customer-destroyed with documentation received | 47 |
| Total recovered or otherwise accounted for | 728 |

Documented implantation status, returns, or customer-certified destruction have accounted for all 1,140 distributed units. Following reconciliation, recall effectiveness checks—including outreach to non-responding accounts and distributor verification—produced a final effectiveness rate of 98.6%. The outstanding 1.4% consists of accounts where alternate records, including shipment, email delivery, and distributor contact documentation, confirmed receipt of the recall communication, but no completed response form was received despite repeated follow-up.

The investigation determined that the coating adhesion condition was caused by plasma-spray parameter drift after an October 2021 chamber maintenance event at the Cork facility. More specifically, Chamber 3 was placed back into production without sufficient confirmation that its operating parameters continued to fall within the validated ranges for applying the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating. Review of batch records and retained samples supported the determination that the condition was confined to the affected lot range.

Corrective and preventive measures were administered under CAPA-2022-0091. These measures comprised recertification of Chamber 3, revalidation of the relevant plasma-spray operating window, stronger verification after maintenance activities, updated maintenance-release documentation, and more stringent process-control review requirements for coating runs. Quality has confirmed both implementation and effectiveness. CAPA-2022-0091 is now closed.

Regulatory Affairs recommends notifying the FDA District Office that recall effectiveness work and final reconciliation have been completed and requesting closure of Recall No. Z-1418-2022. In accordance with 21 CFR 806.20, recall documentation—including customer notifications, response records, distribution and return reconciliation, investigation materials, CAPA documentation, and FDA correspondence—should be retained. The DHF-linked recall file should be archived in Agile and cross-referenced to the Cork manufacturing investigation and CAPA-2022-0091.

Dana

I am formally returning to the unresolved engineering posture associated with ECO-2019-118. Almost three years have passed since I submitted the original Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, yet the Design History File (DHF) index still fails to accurately state our current position.

The relevant technical background is as follows: during development before Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, we established the wear simulator protocol strictly according to ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, with acetabular component placement tested only at a nominal 45° inclination angle. Reports from Meridian Testing Labs verified acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal nominal conditions, supporting our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as documented in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, running the system at steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—generated severe edge-loading dynamics. Relative to the 45° baseline, the wear simulator results indicated a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates, caused by concentrated contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 called for an immediate change to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to reduce edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles, which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy.

Leadership formally deferred ECO-2019-118 in mid-2019. The rationale given at the time focused on commercial friction, including tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and, most importantly, the time needed for complete mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have interrupted peak production volumes.

My central concern now is that, as of January 2022, three complete years after the 4–6× wear multiplier at steep angles was identified, no design modification has been put into effect. None. The product currently shipped from Warsaw and Cork still uses the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

In addition, when I examined the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week, I found that ECO-2019-118 was labeled "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." That statement is factually wrong and presents an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not depend exclusively on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to control a mechanical wear condition known to arise when the cup tilts beyond 50°.

I propose the following two immediate corrective measures:
1. Reopen the ECO-2019-118 DHF index entry and formally assign it the status "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," while expressly recording that the original ISO 14242 protocol evaluated only 45° inclination and did not assess edge-loading conditions.
2. Bring the cross-functional engineering review team—Quality, Product Management, R&D—back together to determine whether to requalify the modified rim tooling or retain the deferred status permanently in the record.

The edge-loading wear multiplier has been known since early 2019. Keeping the change order in administrative limbo without a definite engineering resolution represents a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

National Sales Meeting 2018
ApexHip Positioning Deck — Speaker Notes

Presenter: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: January 18, 2018
Session: Reconstructive Portfolio Breakout
Distribution: Field Sales and Marketing

Slide 1 — Why Apex, Why Now

Begin with the patient rather than the bearing. In general, the ApexHip patient is an active adult who intends to continue working, traveling, cycling, playing golf, and participating in family life. This gives us an opportunity to present a modern total hip platform built around stability, range of motion, and durable materials.

ClassicHip should not be portrayed as a poor product. It is still an important, proven choice and suits many patients. The message is about choice: ClassicHip is our established metal-on-poly platform, while ApexHip offers surgeons an additional option for an active, appropriately selected patient who values a large-head construct and a contemporary fixation platform.

Suggested line: “Apex expands the conversation beyond simply getting back to walking. It is designed for the patient who wants confidence in movement.”

Slide 2 — Differentiating the Platform

The platform rests on three pillars:

1. Stability through large-head options. Apex provides head sizes ranging from 36 to 50 mm, enabling surgeons to choose a construct that supports stability and range of motion.

2. Wear performance. During our ISO 14242 bench testing with standard 45-degree cup inclination, Apex showed lower early wear rates than legacy systems. Keep this point connected to those test conditions, and provide the approved leave-behind if a surgeon requests data.

3. Fixation. The acetabular cup features KinetiCoat porous titanium coating, acquired with KBT, to support bone ingrowth and initial fixation.

Do not let the discussion become a head-to-head “winner” debate with every competitor. Naming brands is unnecessary to establish the point. Most competitive systems may provide either a large head or porous coating; Apex combines both features in a coherent system supported by Veridian’s reconstructive organization.

Slide 3 — KinetiCoat: Make It Concrete

Representatives should be able to describe the coating in straightforward terms. KinetiCoat is not paint, and it must never be characterized as paint. It is a porous titanium coating placed on the cup surface, creating a structure intended to support bone ingrowth over time.

Suggested language: “The goal is biologic fixation. KinetiCoat gives the surgeon a porous surface designed to help the patient’s bone engage with the cup.”

Do not characterize this as faster healing, guaranteed fixation, or superior fixation in every patient. Consistently use “designed to support” and “intended to promote.”

Slide 4 — Handling the Longevity Question

This point is important: never promise a particular number of years. Although we have bench data and a strong engineering rationale, Apex’s clinical follow-up remains short. Do not tell a surgeon or patient that Apex will last 20 years, 25 years, or “a lifetime.”

If asked, say: “Apex was designed with durability in mind, and the available bench testing supports its wear-performance profile. As with any newer system, long-term clinical follow-up continues to accumulate.”

Do not use a ClassicHip survivorship number as an Apex claim. These are different products, and surgeons will recognize that.

Slide 5 — Close

The request is straightforward: find the appropriate surgeon and patient profile, begin with stability, discuss wear performance under the validated test condition, and explain the KinetiCoat fixation advantages. Remain confident and specific while staying within the approved language.

When a question extends beyond the field guide materials, do not improvise. Forward it to Product Marketing or Clinical Affairs, and we will return an answer quickly.
